name: The right of self-preservation as the sole limit on obedience to the sovereign
plain_explanation: Even though Hobbes gives the sovereign nearly unlimited power, he makes one major exception: because the whole point of government is self-preservation, subjects retain an absolute right to defend their own lives, even against the sovereign -- for instance, a right to refuse to fight in war -- though resistance in defense of someone else remains wrong.
precise_definition: Russell's summary: 'The right of self-preservation he regards as absolute, and subjects have the right of self-defence, even against monarchs... he holds (though with limitations) that a man has a right to refuse to fight when called upon by the government to do so. This is a right which no modern government concedes... resistance to the sovereign is only justified in self-defence; resistance in defence of another is always culpable.'
why_it_mattered: It is the one logically necessary exception to Hobbes's absolutism, since self-preservation is the very motive Hobbes gives for instituting government in the first place, and it also explains and justifies Hobbes's own submission to Cromwell once Charles II could no longer protect him.
historical_origin: Set out in the chapter on the liberty of subjects in Leviathan.
examples: Hobbes's own submission to Cromwell during Charles II's exile, on the ground that a sovereign who cannot protect his subjects has no claim on their obedience
Liberty defined as 'the absence of external impediments to motion,' compatible with necessity, as water is 'free' to flow downhill
